Canadian Travelers Face New U.S. Visa Restrictions Under State Department’s Tourism Crackdown

By  Ethan Cotler
Updated  Sep 25, 2026, 2:57 PM EDT
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 6:11

Ethan Cotler is a travel writer who specializes in arts travel. His passion for the arts began when he interned at a local art gallery in high school, and he has gone on to visit museums around the world, including the Van Gogh Museum in Amsterdam, Calouste Gulbenkian Museum in Lisbon, and the Louvre in Paris.

Since then, he has visited several museums in the United States, developing a strong interest in classical paintings.

Prior to contributing to TheTravel, Ethan contributed to the Boston Globe and The Daily Beast, where he offered readers insights from things to do around Boston for the Globe to reporting on the Louvre jewlery heist for the Beast. When he is not writing, he can often be found exploring art galleries and his nose in coffee table books about painters and visual artists.

This article was updated on September 25 at 2:57 p.m. ET with a background from a State Department spokesperson

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has announced new legislation imposing additional U.S. visa restrictions that could affect Canadian travelers. Specifically, the crackdown targets those who engage in “birth tourism.”

Birth tourism is when a parent enters the country to give birth there and secure citizenship and a U.S. passport for their child. This comes as the Trump Administration’s latest attack against the practice.

In July, White House officials were reportedly considering banning pregnant travelers altogether. In late June, the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) increased its investigations into birth tourism. Now, a policy directly targets the practice.

New U.S. Passport Rule For Travelers Under 18 Could Enforce Checks On Parents

A new bill proposed by President Trump could mean parents need to prove their own citizenship when applying for their child's passport.

By  Jasmine Gillett
Sep 2, 2026

New U.S. Visa Restrictions Could Impact Canadian Travelers

The State Department head announced the new restrictions, adding that the policy targets both people who engage (or have previously engaged) in birth tourism and those who facilitate it.

“Today, I am announcing a new visa restriction policy under Section 212(a)(3)(C) of the Immigration and Nationality Act. This policy targets individuals who knowingly engage in, have engaged in, or facilitate birth tourism to the United States, including owners, operators, and managers of commercial birth tourism facilitation networks, visa ‘fixers’ who coach applicants to commit fraud, foreign medical providers who knowingly abet and facilitate such travel and the fraudulent use of our Medicaid system, and other individuals who support, abet, and enable commercial birth tourism,” Rubio said in a statement.

A State Department spokesperson told TheTravel the policy will be applied on a case-by-case basis, adding that it could also target immediate family members. The department also cited its establishment of the "Birth Tourism Prevention Task Force," which revokes visas of people engaging in or facilitating the practice.

The spokesperson told TheTravel that the department has identified cases of birth tourism involving people from every region around the world.

In the announcement, Rubio added that some networks charge travelers tens of thousands of dollars to give birth in the United States to obtain citizenship. According to think tank Migration Policy Institute, the cost can range anywhere from $20,000 to $100,000. It also cited a census-based estimate placing around 22,000 to 26,000 babies born annually in the U.S. as part of birth tourism.

This is less than 1% of the over 3.6 million births in the U.S. in 2024, according to a report from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). Chinese nationals are among the top demographics the federal government has targeted for these schemes.

In 2024, Michael Wei Yueh Liu and his wife, Phoebe Dong, were sentenced to 41 months in prison after prosecutors found them guilty of one count of conspiracy and 10 counts of international money laundering connected to operating a California maternity house for pregnant women from China.

Prosecutors said the couple assisted over 100 pregnant Chinese women in traveling to the U.S. and coached them on how to fool immigration authorities. While Canadians engaging in birth tourism in the U.S. isn’t as common, it has been documented previously.

Canadians Have Been Reported To Engage In Birth Tourism In The U.S.

A 2002 report in the Canadian newspaper The Globe and Mail touched on the practice of Canadians entering the U.S. to obtain dual citizenship for their children.

At the time, Bill Strasberg, a spokesman for the now-defunct Immigration and Naturalization Service (INS), spoke on the topic to the outlet.

"It's something we're very aware of at our southern border, but I haven't heard much about this sort of thing from the Canadian side," Strasberg said.

The INS has since been split into three separate agencies: U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS), U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), and U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP).

Mike Gilhooly, who was an agent for the defunct agency at the time, gave a different account, affirming that his office was "aware that it does happen on the Canadian border, but it hasn't been a growing phenomenon.”

"If people do it on false pretences, by claiming they're on vacation but coming to give birth, we treat it the same as somebody who says they're just visiting but is really there to work," he added.

Canadians seeking U.S. citizenship must immigrate to the U.S. and apply for a green card, which would make them a permanent resident. The process can take anywhere from several months to over a decade.

On the other hand, a Canadian giving birth on U.S. soil would skip that entire process for their child. However, some U.S. lawmakers have been proposing even stricter rules targeting birth tourism.

A Congressman Introduced A Bill Banning Entry To Pregnant Foreigners

Tennessee Congressman Andy Ogles introduced a bill called the "Anchors Away Act," which, if passed, would ban pregnant women from entering the country if they are not U.S. citizens or green card holders.

“What this bill does is, if you are a pregnant woman, you can’t come into this country. Got to be a citizen to be here; you have to be a green card holder. So, if you’re pregnant and you don’t have one of those statuses, no admittance allowed,” the Republican said in a post on X in June.

Other officials share similar views to Ogles. Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche said that "birth tourism" should be viewed as illegal.

“Everybody should agree that it’s a violation of our laws if your intent in coming here, if you’re pregnant, is to have a child to become a U.S. citizen,” Blanche told reporters. “And so what we have to do as the Department of Justice is make sure our agents, our HSI agents that we work with, and the FBI are focused on stopping that.”

The DOJ previously released a memo asking U.S. attorneys to work with the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to "prioritize the investigation and prosecution of birth tourism schemes."

The memo said most cases could be prosecuted as visa fraud; it also said prosecutors should consider several others:

DOJ Suggested Charges For 'Birth Tourism' Schemes

Visa Fraud, 18 U.S.C. § 1546

Wire Fraud and Conspiracy to Commit Wire Fraud, 18 U.S.C. §§ 1343, 1349

Money Laundering and Conspiracy to Commit Money Laundering, 18 U.S.C. § 1956

Unlawful Use of Means of Identification, 18 U.S.C. § 1028(a)(7)

Aggravated Identity Theft, 18 U.S.C. § 1028A(a)(1)

Conspiracy to Commit Health Care Fraud, 18 U.S.C. § 1347

For travelers looking to engage in birth tourism, the U.S. continues to clamp down, and it could result in visa penalties.
